project_tracker_diagnostic: Tall perennial with conspicuously winged/decurrent stems and many white heads; famous for extruding ice ribbons in winter.

project_inclusion.learning_reason: Common or useful Central Texas fall/white composite for field learning.

morphology_keys.habit: Tall herbaceous perennial, often 1–2.2 m in regional Williamson County specimens, robust 1–several unbranched lower stems beneath a much-branched terminal flowering canopy.
morphology_keys.leaves: Usually alternate (lower-most sometimes opposite), simple, rough-hairy / scabrous, often elliptic to ovate or lance-elliptic, with long tapering sessile/petiolar bases extending down the stem as wings; edges often coarsely toothed but can be almost entire. Larger mid-stem leaves and variable sizes—do not key entirely on individual leaf outline.
morphology_keys.heads: Terminal branched flat to domed clusters with dozens of very small white radiate composite heads, often 60–100+ heads. Each head usually only (0–)1–3(–5) short white ray florets around about 8–13 off-white to cream disc florets in regional populations. NOT a big daisy-like head.
morphology_keys.phyllaries: Outer narrow green bracts in 1–2 series beneath each tiny head; UT Williamson describes ca. 5 main outer phyllaries, ~2–2.5 mm long. Receptacular paleae wrap the disc florets, so examine with a hand lens if separating close relatives.
morphology_keys.fruit: Winged flattened cypselae (achenes), ca. 4–6 mm in Williamson populations, with TWO straight persistent bristlelike pappus AWNS ~1.5–3 mm; not 'pappus reduced or absent'. Papery lateral fruit wings are distinct from stem wings.
best_field_traits: alternately attached rough leaves with tapering/decurrent bases
tall perennial with many white very-small heads in flat/panicled canopy
each white head typically just 1–3 little ray florets (not a large daisy)
ice ribbons around split old lower stems after first hard freezes (seasonal bonus)
morphology_keys.stems: Thick pale-to-deep green lower stem frequently with conspicuous vertical WINGS decurrent from leaf bases. UT Williamson: wavy thin wings ca. 3–5.5 mm wide; stems short-hirsute with a white solid pith. Wings can become reduced/lost on aging woody basal portions; inspect intact green internodes.
morphology_keys.rays_vs_disc: Ray FLORETS: few, each white and strap-shaped, pistillate. DISC FLORETS: several small tubular florets, bisexual, cream/white. A 'flower head' is a capitulum containing multiple individual florets.
morphology_keys.frost_flower: During some early freezes, water supplied from still-active roots emerges through cracks in dying lower stem and freezes into delicate ice ribbons; duration is short and occurrence is weather-dependent. Not all plants or freezing mornings show this.
field_id_sequence: 1. Find a sturdy undamaged GREEN internode and follow a leaf base downward into a thin undulating stem wing.
2. Check alternate rough-haired leaves, coarse tooth/entire variability, tapering blade bases.
3. Confirm terminal branched clusters made of numerous TINY whitish flower heads, not a few large heads.
4. Magnify one capitulum: few small white ray FLORETS plus cream tubular disc FLORETS and green phyllaries.
5. In winter, inspect lower living/dead stems after suitable freezes for ice ribbons, but do NOT make their absence a negative ID.
6. On fruiting plants, look for flattened winged cypsela with two pappus awns; true macro required for teaching photo.

look_here_first: LOOK AT THE STEM FIRST: broad, wavy leaflike WINGS run vertically DOWN from the leaf base along the green stem. Follow a leaf to its decurrent ridges with your finger. Then check ALTERNATE rough toothed leaves and a broad autumn canopy of MANY TINY white composite heads (usually only 1–3 white rays per head). Winter ICE RIBBONS at split bases are memorable but seasonal—not required for ID.

confused_with: Verbesina alternifolia (external field look-alike, not installed in local 3-species group)
Ageratina havanensis (white mistflower, a different composite genus)
comparisons.key_distinctions: V. virginica: white heads with only a few short ray florets, many-head flowering canopy, and WINGED leafy stems. V. lindheimeri: opposite/mostly opposite leaves, short non-winged stems, usually a SINGLE BIG YELLOW head with ~13 long rays. V. encelioides: annual, often coarse gray-green triangular leaves and large YELLOW heads, stems generally NOT winged. V. alternifolia can also have winged stems but yellow (not white) heads; ice ribbons alone do not establish V. virginica identification. Ageratina has white discoid fluffy heads without showy white ray florets and no winged stems.
field_cautions: Do not call all wingstem species frostweed: V. alternifolia has winged stems but yellow flower heads.
Do not use frost-flower ice display as a guaranteed or unique species test; weather and other genera matter.
Do not label capillary or cold-weather ice as a 'flower' of the plant; it is water ice.
White-looking tiny rays may be missing on some frostweed heads, so inspect several capitula.
